t: The Tuareg, who call themselves Imuhagh, Kel Tamasheq (“speakers of Tamasheq”) and Kel Tagelmust (“veiled people”), are an Amazigh people whose founding queen, Tin Hinan, is believed to have lived in the 4th or 5th century.

Organised in confederations under an amenokal and ranked into nobles, vassals, clerics, artisans and enslaved people, they controlled trans-Saharan trade routes and ran salt caravans across the desert.
The Tuareg resisted French conquest from 1881 to 1920; after independence their homeland was divided among five states, and uprisings followed in Mali and Niger from the 1960s.
dyk: Among the Tuareg it is the men, not the women, who traditionally veil their faces: a man takes on the tagelmust when he reaches maturity, as a rite of passage to manhood.
ev: Tin Hinan, the Tuareg founding queen, leads her people south into the Sahel; her tomb stands at Abalessa in the Hoggar
Islam reaches North Africa with the Umayyad Caliphate, and the Tuareg in time adopt it
A Tuareg ruling house founds the Sultanate of Agadez in the Aïr Mountains
Tuareg fighters annihilate the French expedition led by Paul Flatters
The French defeat the Kel Ahaggar at the Battle of Tit
After a clash at Tchin-Tabaraden, Tuareg in Mali and Niger rise and claim independence for their homeland
Peace agreements in Mali and Niger decentralise power and bring Tuareg fighters into the national armies
During the Mali War the Azawad Liberation Front captures Kidal and parts of Gao

f.homeland: The Sahara and Sahel from southwestern Libya and southern Algeria to Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso and northern Nigeria, with the Kinnin in Chad and Sudan; the Ahaggar and Aïr mountains, the Adrar des Iforas, Kidal, Agadez, Timbuktu and Ghat; an estimated 1.2 to 3 million people, about 2 million of them in Niger, the majority in Mali’s Kidal Region.
f.period: Tin Hinan, the founding queen, 4th–5th century; Islam from the 7th century and the Maliki school from the 16th; the Sultanate of Agadez from 1449; confederations under an amenokal by the 19th century; French conquest from 1881 to 1920; the homeland divided among independent states in the 1960s; uprisings in the 1960s, from 1990 to 1996, from 2007 and in the Mali War.
f.known: the tagelmust, the indigo veil worn by men; the Tifinagh script; trans-Saharan salt caravans; confederations led by an amenokal; ranks of nobles, vassals, clerics, artisans and enslaved people; matrilineal descent and the woman’s tent; silver jewellery and the Agadez Cross; the anzad violin, the tende drum and the guitar music of Tinariwen
f.sources: accounts by Ibn Hawkal (10th century), El-Bekri, Edrisi, Ibn Battutah, Leo Africanus and Ibn Khaldûn; the Tin Hinan tomb at Abalessa and its Tifinagh inscription; travellers such as James Richardson (1845–1846); Charles de Foucauld’s dictionary and collections of poetry; anthropologists and linguists such as Susan Rasmussen, Jeffrey Heath and Karl-Gottfried Prasse; French colonial reports; genetic studies.
